title: Drawdowns, Diversification, and the Hidden Risks in Today’s Markets - Systematic Investor - Ep. 354

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Drawdowns, Diversification, and the Hidden Risks in Today’s Markets - Systematic Investor - Ep. 354.docx

speakers: Rob Carver (independent systematic trader and author)
summary: Top Traders Unplugged Ep.354 (late June 2025): Rob Carver on his largest live drawdown, factor and PCA views of trend, Kelly sizing and skew, blending discretionary forecasts, and Ilmanen's paper on bond contrarian vs equity extrapolation. Conclusions: size by Sharpe-consistent vol, trend works where consensus mean-reversion expectations fail, trend timing is too weak to exploit.

coverage.note: intro, weather, Asness podcast recommendation; nothing actionable

container volume reversal, June trend weakness, oil whipsaw, drawdown vs history, low system risk
positions, Sharpe-unit view of drawdown, skew rule of thumb, equity perspective
short-term index in June, factor decomposition question, asset-class index construction
trending an asset class index, PCA of crypto and equities, metals factors
residual relative momentum, 70/30 split of index vs residual

industry sameness, AHL history and hiring; nothing actionable
Renaissance hiring, marginal gains, portfolio optimisation, mistakes
liquidity vanishing, IP contamination and staff moves

best/worst days argument, trend versus day timing, simulations

completeness_estimate: 0.94 - first reader captured essentially all of Carver's methods and numbers; missed Black-Litterman, the luck caveat on manager dispersion, analyst optimism bias and the risk-premium argument, plus two small attribution/emphasis errors.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they plan to roll back an important capital rule that gives banks um that they have had to comply with to limit their ability to hold more treasuries
claims.claim: The Fed plans to roll back a bank capital rule that limited Treasury holdings, which raises bank demand for Treasuries but sets up risk of another bank crisis.
claims.indicator: bank capital rule on Treasury holdings
claims.direction: Treasury demand up, bank risk up

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the the Basel 2 um banking um capital adequacy rules were partly responsible for the last financial crisis
claims.claim: Capital adequacy rules can cause crises (Basel 2 contributed to 2008), so loosening or treating Bitcoin and stablecoins as bank assets is a risk Rob is concerned about.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: containers and boxes. You know, how much is being shipped uh in and out of the US
claims.claim: Container and box shipping data (Bank of America box survey) has been a strong predictor of the US economy in recent years.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Okay now we're 3 months later now 61% believe they're going to fall more likely than rise
claims.claim: Box price expectations fell sharply: in March 11% of respondents said prices were more likely to fall; by June 61%, signalling weakening demand.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a 6.9% decrease in inbound US volume last month. Um which is um a big reversal from the 11% and almost 10% increase we saw in March and April
claims.claim: US inbound container volume rose about 10-11% in March-April (front-loading before tariffs) then fell 6.9% in May.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the big surge initially after the uh strike on Iran and then the collapse uh only a few days ago
claims.claim: June 2025 trend returns were choppy (one step forward, one back); the oil surge after the Iran strike and collapse days later whipsawed trend followers; trend barometer at 43.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: this the current draw down is the largest I've seen in live trading, and it's it's kind of on a par with the biggest draw downs in my back test, which go back to 1970
claims.claim: Rob's current drawdown is his largest live and about equal to his worst backtest drawdowns since 1970, a one-in-10 to one-in-20 year event.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: my own system disagrees with that and is saying, well, actually still pretty low risk to be honest
claims.claim: Rob's trend signals were weak in mid-2025 (long equities, a little short bonds, flat energies), so the system took low risk instead of piling on positions.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I'm short gas but I'm long crude so um you know I'm kind of I could have sort of hedge position in energies effectively
claims.claim: Rob's energy position is net flat (short gas, long crude), with no big risk coming on.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: convert your P&L into an annualized sharp ratio
claims.claim: Expressing P&L as an annualised Sharpe ratio gives intuition for drawdowns: Rob is at -1.3 Sharpe units for 2025 against a long-run Sharpe of 0.5-1.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: in a good year I'll make two sharp duration units. bad lose one
claims.claim: Trend following is positively skewed at the right time frequency: a good year is about +2 Sharpe units, a bad year about -1.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: when the S&P 500 is down 50 or 60% in which what we've seen in the last 25 years, that's like four four standard deviation of the annualized volatility
claims.claim: A one standard deviation drawdown for trend is small compared with equity bear markets of about four standard deviations.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: even strategies that don't make money for a while might still be a good strategy to have in your portfolio
claims.claim: A strategy can be worth holding through a flat spell if it delivers uncorrelated returns in the long run.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: short-term traders index is down 3% in June and now it's down 5 1/2% in uh for the year
claims.claim: Short-term CTAs were hit in June 2025 by news-driven reversals after doing well in April, despite trading at one third of trend followers' volatility.
claims.indicator: short-term traders index vs trend index

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I kind of normalize everything by volatility and then equally weight
claims.claim: Rob builds an asset-class index equally weighted by volatility (US weight about 10% not 70% as in a cap-weighted index) to act as a factor.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: what I then do is say, well, I'm going to trend follow that index
claims.claim: Trend signal on the asset-class index is applied to every instrument, equivalent to trading a metals or equity factor (all long or all short).
claims.direction: Long all metals when index up

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: 70% of the weight was coming from Bitcoin. So basically you know crypto you can think of as Bitcoin plus noise effectively
claims.claim: PCA of crypto shows 70% weight on Bitcoin; in equities PCA and cap weights give similar index; other asset classes are less clear.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: precious metals like gold, silver, platinum that act as kind of riskoff assets like you know Swiss exchange rates and US treasuries
claims.claim: Metals have two drivers: precious metals as a risk-off factor and industrial metals tied to growth, so a PCA would likely give two factors.
claims.direction: Precious up on risk-off; industrials up on growth

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: we'd have a relative value strategy on top of that where we'd go long gold and short silver and then add everything up at the end
claims.claim: After trading the index, add a market-neutral residual momentum: long assets beating the vol-normalised index over six months, short underperformers.
claims.indicator: vol-normalised outperformance vs asset class index

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: In the very long run, it mean reverts and in the very short term, it mean reverts
claims.claim: Residual momentum trends at about one-month holding periods but mean-reverts at very short and very long horizons.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you find that the splits about 7030
claims.claim: Index plus residual trend gives results almost identical to plain trend following; about 70% of profit comes from trending the asset-class index and 30% from relative trends.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you just trade that, you know, you're probably going to be getting about 70% of the performance as if you traded everything on top
claims.claim: A limited-capital investor can trade only the main instrument per asset class (S&P, 5-10 year bond, gold or metals) and get about 70% of the performance.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: once you start factoring those out as well, you will get to the point potentially where you've got a mean reverting residual, which means you can create a mean reversing strategy
claims.claim: Removing more principal components could leave a mean-reverting residual that supports a mean-reversion strategy.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you can run a PCA entire futures universe. So actually equities, bonds, everything together
claims.claim: A PCA across the whole futures universe could be used as a trading strategy, not just a risk tool.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if there's only a few factors driving everything well we just need to trade those factors we don't need the other hundred or so instruments
claims.claim: The replication argument says a few factors explain CTA performance, so those can be traded alone; Rob notes this is PCA of trend returns not of markets.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you should run your your um system um at a standard deviation equal to SH ratio
claims.claim: Full Kelly says run annualised volatility equal to Sharpe ratio to maximise CAGR, assuming Gaussian returns, known Sharpe and infinite leverage; at Sharpe 0.5 that is 50% vol.
claims.conditions: Gaussian returns, known Sharpe, unlimited leverage

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: most CTAs, hedge funds are running an even lower vault than I am as well
claims.claim: Practical volatility targets (Rob's is under half of Kelly) are well below full Kelly because the Sharpe is uncertain.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: If you've got negatively skewed returns, you need to run at a lower volt target. And if you've got positively skewed returns, you should run at a higher volt target
claims.claim: Negative skew requires a lower Kelly-type volatility target and positive skew a higher one.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it doesn't actually improve um increase your standard deviation as much as you think it your standard deviation target as much as you think it does
claims.claim: Positive skew raises the optimal volatility target by less than people think, so it cannot be converted into higher returns easily.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if if volatility increases then I you know reduce my position size throughout the life of a trade
claims.claim: Position sizing studies (Saratini and Quantica) find that both volatility-adjusting positions during a trade and scaling with forecast strength help in a long backtest, with small differences.

correction.issue: Says differences are small between both sizing adjustments; Carver says the differences are not massive but that pyramiding (scaling position with forecast strength) has a much bigger effect than volatility adjustment.
correction.fix: Position sizing studies (Saratini and Quantica) find that both volatility-adjusting positions during a trade and scaling with forecast strength help over a long backtest; differences are not large, but scaling with forecast strength (pyramiding) has the bigger effect.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: as a rule of thumb if you can get a higher sharp you can get a higher CAGR assuming you've got leverage um unless you give up too much positive skew in the process of doing it
claims.claim: Higher Sharpe gives higher CAGR with leverage unless it costs too much positive skew.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: that does give you extra positive skew but you you lose too much in sharp ratio
claims.claim: Fixed-stop sizing that ignores changing volatility adds positive skew but loses too much Sharpe, giving lower CAGR.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: at a portfolio level um you know all that's going to do is increase the dispersion of your trades
claims.claim: Letting winners run (cocoa anecdote) is anecdotal bias; at the portfolio level it increases dispersion and concentration, so a reversal causes big losses.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: allow your portfolio to become too concentrated in one place then the standard deviation is going to be a lot higher
claims.claim: Concentration lifts portfolio volatility above the intended target, so the manager is over-risked at peaks.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the volatility of that product or that fund uh reached something like 90% at times because of the static position sizing
claims.claim: A well-known trend manager with static sizing reached about 90% volatility, which implies a belief in a Sharpe of 0.9 or more, about twice a realistic 0.5.

correction.issue: Attributes the Sharpe implication to Niels; Niels only says the fund's volatility reached about 90% because of static sizing. The inference that 90% vol implies an expected Sharpe of 0.9 (about twice a realistic 0.5) is Carver's, from Kelly sizing.
correction.fix: Niels: a well-known trend manager using static position sizing saw fund volatility reach about 90% at times. Carver: under Kelly sizing that implies an expected Sharpe of 0.9 or more, about twice a realistic 0.5.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you think your risk is now 90% that implies you think your current expected sharp 0.9
claims.claim: Nobody can forecast near-term Sharpe accurately enough to justify doubling the risk target.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: essentially the way my system works is I convert everything into a forecast and a forecast is just a number and it's a scaled number
claims.claim: Rob scales every signal into a forecast from -20 to +20 (10 = average bullish) so systematic and discretionary views can be combined.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: use some kind of weighted average of, you know, what what those discretionary forecasts are combined with your more systematic forecasts
claims.claim: Discretionary forecasts on the same scale can be blended with systematic ones using weights (50/50, 70/30), which Rob calls semi-automatic trading.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: because the forecast is a number, you can actually then independently verify how good that forecast is in exactly the same way you could verify a back test
claims.claim: A numeric forecast can be tested like a backtest, so the weight on discretionary views can be based on evidence.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: systematic methods of forecasting volatility are extremely good and I don't I think it's tough to beat that
claims.claim: Do not apply discretionary views to volatility forecasts because systematic forecasts are hard to beat.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: setting stop-loss limits for your stop losses and and and things like you know optimizing a portfolio for the the most diversification those things should all be done scientifically I believe using systematic methods
claims.claim: Only the buy-or-not decision may be discretionary; sizing, holding period, stops and portfolio optimisation should be systematic, as done by Marshall Wace feeding forecasts into an optimiser.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: hiring people from you know mainly pure mathematics backgrounds with with no finance experience because they want to look at the data with fresh eyes
claims.claim: Renaissance hires pure mathematicians without finance experience to see the data with fresh eyes, while others hire from the same schools.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you could give the same data and the same books to a bunch of people and ask them to do to create you know a trading strategy um and they'd all do it in slightly different ways
claims.claim: Skilled managers differ in small details such as beta cleaning; there is no big undiscovered secret, only marginal gains in execution and data cleaning.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: things like sort of optimizing portfolios to try and make the best use of this vast variety of of markets we've
claims.claim: Cost-aware portfolio optimisation across many illiquid markets separates the profitable from less profitable managers.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: trading too quickly you know overconentrating individual markets
claims.claim: Rob's mistakes were trading too quickly and over-concentrating, and he stresses avoiding errors.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: market capacity can vanish like that right and it did in 2009
claims.claim: Liquidity in OTC markets can vanish suddenly (fixed income agencies in 2009).

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I can't imagine you know someone leaving say a big CTA going to the big CTA and taking some big big secret with them
claims.claim: IP leakage between CTAs is minor; staff moves bring a fresh perspective, though less systematic and higher frequency strategies rely more on secrets.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Then that obviously is a fantastic place to do trend following
claims.claim: Trend following works where consensus expects mean reversion and is wrong, and mean reversion works where consensus expects trends and is wrong.
claims.testable: yes - compare forecast errors with trend returns

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: people think that interest rates are going to uh mean revert and they don't they don't mean revert they persist for long periods of time
claims.claim: Forecasts always assume rates return to normal (4% expected from 2009 to 2020, falling from 6% in 1999), but rates persist, which favours bond trend.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: They think if times are good, they're going to continue getting good. If times are bad, they're going to continue getting bad
claims.claim: Equity analysts extrapolate, so momentum is already priced in and even overpriced.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: trend falling in bonds has done very well indeed trend following in equities has done much less well in equity indices
claims.claim: Trend works better in bonds than equity indices because investors expect mean reversion in bonds and extrapolate in equities, and equity trend suffers V-shaped reversals.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: carry tends to be higher in bonds and u that means that you will earn carry which creates a secular upward trend in bond prices
claims.claim: Bond carry and secular decline in rates, plus rising equity valuations, give a tailwind to momentum that is stronger in bonds.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: where you know where does the money come from, right?
claims.claim: Ask who is on the other side of a risk premium trade (Ilmanen): knowing the counterparty helps judge whether a factor persists.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: equity returns are also negatively skewed and the worst days are much worse than the best days are good
claims.claim: Avoiding the worst days beats missing the best days because equity returns are negatively skewed, so Asness's critique of the 'missing the best days' argument holds.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: over the last 3 months the market has been trending down therefore I think I should no longer be owning the market
claims.claim: Trend-based exposure changes are different from forecasting one-day moves; nobody sits out single days.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: increase the dispersion of your returns over time and that's what his statistical work shows
claims.claim: Simulations of randomly missing days raise dispersion of returns, reinforcing the case against day-timing; costs and taxes add to the damage.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: some of the best returns actually comes after your worst returns uh period
claims.claim: Trend followers' best returns often follow their worst, so stay invested and hope for a rebound in 2025.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: If trend following had had a good year and there was a positive autocorrelation between annual returns and trend following then you should if there's been a good year you should invest more
claims.claim: Timing entry into trend following needs autocorrelation of strategy returns: positive would mean add after good years, negative the reverse.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: performance fees actually make your returns more negatively autocorrelated um because you only take performance fees out of um when you're doing well
claims.claim: Performance fees bias net returns toward negative autocorrelation, so autocorrelation tests should use gross returns.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: for momentum specifically if I looked at um say annual returns I did find there was a bit of weak pos positive autocorrelation
claims.claim: Gross momentum returns show weak positive annual autocorrelation that disappears at longer horizons.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you would really be crazy to try and use them in any kind of momentum market timing strategy because they would definitely get eaten up by fee fees or costs
claims.claim: The autocorrelation effects are too weak to time trend following; strategy timing is as hard as market timing.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there was seminal paper written by Black Litterman in the early '9s, I think, where they they basically took the kind of standard portfolio construction technology
claims.claim: Black-Litterman is the classic framework for blending discretionary return views into a systematic (e.g. market-cap) portfolio; Carver's simpler alternative is a weighted average of scaled forecasts.
claims.testable: yes - blended portfolios can be backtested against pure systematic

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: If you look at the profitable managers and the less profitable managers, because there's a lot of luck, right? See, they may it's not necessarily whether they're good or bad. I think you can it's hard to tell.
claims.claim: Return differences between CTAs are largely luck, so it is hard to tell skilled from unskilled managers from outcomes; post-mortems should ask whether a loss came from bad luck or a bad decision such as overweighting an illiquid market.
claims.testable: partly - skill vs luck tests on manager track records need long histories

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: analysts generally are overoptimistic and there are institutional biases as to why that might be the case
claims.claim: Equity analysts' EPS forecasts carry a systematic optimism bias from institutional incentives, which shrank somewhat after post-tech-bubble reforms; this level bias is separate from their extrapolation bias.
claims.indicator: analyst EPS growth forecasts vs realised
claims.conditions: bias smaller after the early-2000s reforms
claims.testable: yes - IBES forecast errors over time

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I'm happy with the thesis that if you have increased risk you'll get higher returns equities are quite risky therefore if you're investing for the long term buy
claims.claim: The honest case for long-only equities is the long-run risk premium (higher risk, higher return), not the 'missing the best days' argument, which is marketing.
claims.conditions: long holding period; cannot time the market
